title: Transmission-based precautions and isolation
blurb: Match contact, droplet and airborne precautions to the organism, and decide who gets the single room.
question: A medical ward has one free single room. Four patients need one: which should the nurse in charge prioritise, using the national IPC manual's principles?

teach.h: When standard precautions are not enough
teach.body: Transmission-based precautions (TBPs) are extra measures added on top of standard precautions when a patient has a known or suspected infection or colonisation. They are grouped by how the organism travels: contact, droplet or airborne. Some organisms use more than one route. The choice rests on the suspected organism, how severe the illness is, its route, and the setting and procedures involved, with advice from the infection prevention and control team (IPCT).

An inpatient in any hospital in the UK or abroad, or a known link to a CPE carrier.
Known or suspected infection or colonisation.
Document the placement decision in the notes and pass it on at every handover.

teach.caption: Single-room prioritisation is reviewed daily. If the door cannot stay closed, record a risk assessment.

teach.body: Use single-use items where possible and dedicate reusable equipment to the room, decontaminating it before anyone else uses it. Clean the room at least daily with 1,000 ppm available chlorine (or detergent then 1,000 ppm). Transfer the patient elsewhere only if clinically necessary, ask them to wear an FRSM in communal areas if tolerated, and tell the receiving department and porters what precautions are needed. Signage should limit entry without breaching confidentiality.

teach.h: Worked scenario: one room, four patients
teach.body: On Ward 6, nurse in charge Grace has one single room. Mr Doyle, 70, has new vomiting and diarrhoea and suspected norovirus; Mrs Sato has a healed wound and is MRSA-negative; Mr Ellis has a urinary tract infection; Ms Ruiz has a non-productive cough from heart failure. Grace moves Mr Doyle into the room with contact precautions, informs the IPCT and records the decision. Norovirus spreads rapidly through a bay, so he is the greatest cross-infection risk. She reviews the room allocation again the next day.

teach.text: Do not confuse the 1 metre droplet distance with a 2 metre rule: the NIPCM returned to 1 metre in all areas. And do not put an FFP3 respirator on the infectious patient: the patient wears an FRSM as source control; staff wear FFP3 for airborne organisms.

items: TBPs are added to SICPs: contact (commonest), droplet (at least 1 metre), airborne.
Assess infection risk on arrival and document placement; review single rooms daily.
Prioritise single rooms for excessive cough, diarrhoea and vomiting, and MDROs.
Cohort patients with the same confirmed infection (mixed cohorts need a service-pressure plan); never the immunosuppressed.
Transfer only if clinically necessary, with an FRSM on the patient and the receiving area informed.

summary: You can now match contact, droplet and airborne precautions to common organisms and decide who should have a single room or be cohorted. You can also manage transfers, equipment and cleaning for an isolated patient.

A.q: During teaching on transmission-based precautions, a student asks which route causes most cross-infection in healthcare. What is the correct answer?
options: Contact, direct or via surroundings
Droplet spread within 1 metre
Airborne spread through aerosols
Bloodborne spread through sharps injuries
A.why: The NIPCM describes contact transmission, directly or indirectly via the immediate environment and equipment, as the most common route of cross-infection.

whyNot.1: Droplet spread matters for respiratory organisms but is less common than contact overall.
whyNot.2: Airborne organisms such as measles and TB are less common causes of cross-infection than contact.
whyNot.3: Sharps injuries are an occupational risk, not the main route of cross-infection between patients.

A.q: Mrs Patel, 59, has confirmed seasonal influenza and is in a single room under droplet precautions. The nurse needs to take her observations at the bedside. Which mask should the nurse wear?
options: An FFP3 respirator after a fit check
A powered respirator hood
No mask, as gloves and an apron suffice
A fluid-resistant surgical mask
A.why: For droplet precautions, staff wear an FRSM when providing care within 1 metre (NIPCM 2.4). FFP3 is reserved for airborne pathogens and AGPs.

whyNot.0: FFP3 is not needed for routine care under droplet precautions without an AGP.
whyNot.1: A powered hood is an alternative to FFP3 for airborne risks, not routine droplet care.
whyNot.2: Care within 1 metre of a patient on droplet precautions requires an FRSM.

A.q: Which newly admitted patient should be flagged as a possible carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales (CPE) risk?
options: A woman admitted from her own home after a fall downstairs
A man who was an inpatient in a hospital abroad
A man who had chickenpox as a child
A woman with a recent viral sore throat
A.why: The NIPCM flags patients who have been an inpatient in any hospital in the UK or abroad, or who are linked to a CPE carrier, as a cross-infection risk.

whyNot.0: Admission from home after a fall is not itself a CPE risk factor.
whyNot.2: Childhood chickenpox is not linked to CPE carriage.
whyNot.3: A viral sore throat does not indicate CPE risk.

B.q: Single rooms on an elderly care ward are full. Four patients have laboratory-confirmed norovirus. The IPCT agrees a cohort bay. Which arrangement is correct?
options: Place them in a bay with other patients who have diarrhoea of unknown cause
Place them in a bay with the door open to aid ventilation
Spread them between bays to reduce the load in any one area
Place them together in one bay, door closed, with dedicated equipment
B.why: Cohorting is appropriate for two or more patients with the same confirmed infection, separated by at least 1 metre, door closed, with equipment dedicated to the area (NIPCM 2.1, 2.2).

whyNot.0: Cohorts should share the same confirmed infection; unknown diarrhoea could be C. difficile or another organism.
whyNot.1: Isolation and cohort room doors should be kept closed.
whyNot.2: Spreading infected patients exposes more bays and more patients.

B.q: Mr Grant, 74, has a suspected respiratory infection and is in a single room. He needs a CT scan, and a portable scan is not possible. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Delay the scan until he has had 48 hours of antibiotics
Send him with an FFP3 respirator on, if tolerated
Ask him to wear an FRSM if tolerated and inform radiology
Send him without precautions as he will be scanned quickly
B.why: Infectious patients are transferred only if clinically necessary, wearing an FRSM in communal areas if tolerated, and the receiving department must know the precautions needed (NIPCM 2.1).

whyNot.0: A clinically necessary scan should not be delayed; precautions make the transfer safe.
whyNot.1: An infectious patient must never wear an FFP3 respirator, as it filters incoming rather than expelled air.
whyNot.3: The receiving area must be informed and source control used during the transfer.

B.q: Mr Hale, 86, has MRSA and delirium and is nursed in a single room. With the door closed he becomes distressed and has tried to climb out of bed. What should the nurse do?
options: Keep the door closed and increase sedation
Move him to an open bay to calm him
Document a risk assessment and agree a plan with the IPCT
Keep the door closed and check on him less often to settle him
B.why: Isolation room doors should stay closed, but where this is not possible a documented risk assessment is needed. His safety from falls must be balanced with IPC risk, with IPCT advice.

whyNot.0: Sedation to enforce isolation is not appropriate and increases harm from delirium and falls.
whyNot.1: Moving an MRSA-positive patient into a bay without IPCT advice increases cross-infection risk.
whyNot.3: Less frequent observation of a distressed, delirious patient increases falls risk.

C.q: A ward has one single room. Which patient should the nurse in charge prioritise for it?
options: Mrs Allen, 82, with a urinary tract infection and no diarrhoea
Mr Dunn, 66, with stable chronic heart failure and ankle oedema
Ms Carr, 45, with a healing surgical wound and no infection
Mr Bello, 70, with vomiting, diarrhoea and suspected norovirus
C.why: Diarrhoea and vomiting present a high cross-infection risk, and norovirus spreads rapidly, so he takes priority. The decision is documented and reviewed daily (NIPCM 1.1, 2.1).

whyNot.0: A urinary tract infection without diarrhoea carries a low cross-infection risk with SICPs.
whyNot.1: Heart failure is not an infection risk.
whyNot.2: A healing wound without infection does not need isolation.

C.q: Mrs Ross had C. difficile infection and has been discharged from a single room. What should the terminal clean include?
options: Detergent wipe of all surfaces; curtains left in place for the scheduled change
Curtains removed as infectious linen; room cleaned with 1,000 ppm chlorine
Alcohol wipes on surfaces and curtains sprayed with disinfectant
Room cleaned from the most to the least contaminated areas
C.why: Terminal decontamination removes curtains and bedding as infectious linen and cleans with 1,000 ppm available chlorine, high to low and least to most contaminated (NIPCM 2.3).

whyNot.0: Detergent alone is not the terminal clean, and curtains must be removed as infectious linen.
whyNot.2: Alcohol is not effective against C. difficile spores, and curtains are removed rather than sprayed.
whyNot.3: Cleaning runs from least to most contaminated so dirt is not spread to clean areas.

C.q: A care home resident, Mr Ivanov, has suspected influenza. He needs hospital admission for worsening breathing. What must the care home nurse do?
options: Inform the ambulance service and hospital of his infectious status
Keep his infection status private to protect his right to confidentiality
Ask him to wear an FFP3 respirator for the journey
Delay the transfer until a swab result is available
C.why: When a resident with an infection is transferred, the ambulance service and hospital admission area must be informed of their infectious status (NIPCM 2.1).

whyNot.1: Sharing infection status with those providing care is necessary for safety and is not a breach of confidentiality.
whyNot.2: Infectious patients must not wear FFP3; an FRSM if tolerated is used for source control.
whyNot.3: A clinically urgent admission is not delayed for a swab result.

reteach.title: Follow the organism's journey
reteach.question: How does this organism get from one person to the next, and what blocks that path?

blocks.body: Contact organisms ride on hands, surfaces and equipment, so you block them with hand hygiene, gloves and apron, dedicated equipment and cleaning. Droplets fly a short distance, so you add an FRSM within 1 metre and keep beds apart. Airborne particles hang in room air, so you need a negative-pressure room and an FFP3 respirator or powered hood.

blocks.text: Patients wear FRSMs for source control; staff wear FFP3 for airborne risks. An FFP3 on the patient does nothing for the people around them.

explain.body: Most common route. Gloves and apron for contact with the patient or their environment, dedicated equipment, enhanced cleaning. Soap and water hand hygiene for C. difficile and norovirus.

items.label: chlorine for daily isolation room clean

test.q: Which organism is managed with contact precautions in a single en-suite room?
options: Pulmonary tuberculosis (TB)
Measles
Clostridioides difficile
Seasonal influenza
test.why: C. difficile spreads by contact and spores in the environment, so it needs contact precautions in a single en-suite room.

whyNot.0: Pulmonary TB is airborne and needs a negative-pressure room.
whyNot.1: Measles needs droplet and airborne precautions in a negative-pressure room.
whyNot.3: Influenza is managed with droplet precautions.

explain.body: Droplets from the respiratory tract travel a short distance, at least 1 metre. Staff wear an FRSM within 1 metre; cohorted patients are at least 1 metre apart.

test.q: Two patients with the same confirmed respiratory virus are cohorted in a bay. What separation does the NIPCM require between them?
options: At least 1 metre
At least 2 metres
At least 3 metres
A closed curtain
test.why: Cohorted infectious patients are separated by at least 1 metre (3 feet) with the door closed; the COVID-era 2 metres has reverted to 1 metre.

whyNot.1: 2 metres was a temporary COVID-19 measure and no longer applies.
whyNot.2: 3 metres is not the NIPCM distance; it confuses 3 feet with metres.
whyNot.3: A curtain is not a substitute for physical distance.

explain.body: Aerosols spread without close contact. Negative-pressure room where available, door closed, staff in FFP3 respirators or powered hoods, removed outside the room if there is no anteroom.

test.q: Tariq, 30, is admitted with suspected measles. Where should he ideally be placed?
options: A cohort bay with other febrile patients
A single room with the door open
A standard bay near the nurses' station
A negative-pressure isolation room
test.why: NIPCM appendix 11 places measles in a negative-pressure isolation room with FFP3 or hood for staff.

whyNot.0: Cohorting with patients without confirmed measles exposes them to infection.
whyNot.1: Doors must stay closed; an open door lets aerosols escape.
whyNot.2: An open bay allows airborne spread to other patients.

explain.body: Assess on arrival, document placement in notes and handovers, review single rooms daily, transfer only if clinically necessary, inform receiving areas, consider prolonged shedding before ending isolation.

test.q: How often should single-room isolation priorities be reviewed on a ward?
options: Daily
Weekly
On discharge
At each ward audit
test.why: The NIPCM states that single room prioritisation should be reviewed daily, with IPCT advice.

whyNot.1: Weekly review would leave higher-risk patients without a room for too long.
whyNot.2: Review on discharge is too late to reallocate rooms by risk.
whyNot.3: Audit cycles are not frequent enough for patient placement decisions.
